articles.title: TSMC reportedly weighs 20% CoWoS price increase as Nvidia Blackwell and Rubin chips put pressure on packaging capacity — equipment lead times stretch to eight months - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: TSMC reportedly weighs 20% CoWoS price increase as Nvidia Blackwell and Rubin chips put pressure on packaging capacity — equipment lead times stretch to eight months  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
TSMC is weighing raising prices for its Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS) advanced packaging technology by as much as 20%, reports Trendforce, citing supply chain sources and local media. The increase reflects strained capacity amid AI demand and longer delivery times for chipmaking tools. Such a hike would be significant, as CoWoS is already one of the tightest links in the AI supply chain. TSMC has yet to confirm the report.
CoWoS combines logic dies and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks within a single package, which is how AI accelerators get the data bandwidth that demanding workloads require. Building these packages is only getting harder as chip designers cram in more compute and memory. Nvidia’s Blackwell already pairs two large GPU dies with eight HBM3E stacks, whereas the upcoming Rubin and Rubin Ultra are expected to push integration further, which will increase pressure on packaging and the supply chain that supports it.
Testing is turning into another bottleneck. Blackwell reportedly takes three to four times longer to test than Nvidia’s previous-generation Hopper, and Rubin could need as much as seven times longer. Extended test cycles keep equipment occupied for longer, which makes it harder to increase output as demand grows. GPUs are not the only products competing for capacity either, as server CPUs and custom ASICs also need advanced packaging, adding more strain to an already crowded supply chain.
Tools are also taking longer to arrive, as equipment lead times have reportedly stretched from three to six months to as long as eight months, making timely access to fab equipment increasingly important. As a result, TSMC has reportedly placed this year’s equipment orders at existing prices instead of negotiating discounts or extra features — a departure from its customary approach of using its purchasing power to secure better terms. Essentially, getting the tools on time now appears to matter more to the company than getting them cheaply.
The squeeze echoes a report from September, which said that TSMC’s projected semiconductor equipment requirements had almost doubled in six months as the company expanded production to meet AI demand. Cliff Hou, deputy co-COO at TSMC, said that by July the company’s expected equipment needs had reached 1.9 times its original estimate as AI demand accelerated. “Compared with the pattern 30 years ago, we have never seen the demand increase that much, that frequency of changes,” Hou said at the time.
TSMC is also trying to broaden its packaging supply chain. Earlier this month, GlobalFoundries agreed to produce silicon interposers for TSMC’s CoWoS in the U.S. under a five-year contract worth $2 billion, with production expected to ramp up in the first half of 2028. However, interposers are only one part of the packaging flow, so the agreement alone will not eliminate shortages.
Higher costs are not limited to packaging. TSMC is reportedly considering broader price increases for 2027, with wafer prices on advanced process technologies expected to rise by 5% to 10%. Customers using 2nm and 3nm-class nodes could face the steepest hikes, whereas those seeking capacity beyond their original allocations may have to pay additional premiums, which could push some costs up by as much as 25%.

Industry estimates cited by Trendforce put TSMC’s monthly capacity at over 106,000 wafers in 2026, with a target of 227,000 wafers in 2027 as the company works to keep pace with demand for increasingly complex AI processors. If both the packaging and wafer price increases materialize, the cost of AI hardware will likely climb further, and some of that will inevitably be passed down the chain.

articles.title: How Recent Starlink Restrictions Expose Europe’s Dependence on US Military Space Services - Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI)
articles.summary: How Recent Starlink Restrictions Expose Europe’s Dependence on US Military Space Services  Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI)
articles.full_text:
By Mason Hurlocker | 27 October 2026
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not reflect those of any institution with which the author is or may be affiliated.
Summary
- On 14 October 2026, SpaceX reportedly capped the speed at which its military satellite service can operate in Ukraine, disabling Ukrainian interceptor drones and highlighting the degree to which European security relies on a single United States (US)-based provider.
- The following day, the European Commission began preparations to fast-track approval of Project Bromo, a merger of the Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo space businesses intended to create a European alternative to SpaceX.
- A merged ‘champion’ is likely to strengthen Europe’s satellite industry, but it is highly unlikely to close the gap with Starlink before the EU’s own constellation launches in 2029, leaving Ukraine and European militaries mostly dependent on US-controlled services for the rest of the decade.
Context
On 14 October 2026, Starshield terminals, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink service, began losing connectivity in Ukraine at speeds faster than 161 km/h. This cap effectively prevents Ukrainian interceptor drones from engaging Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones, and has also disrupted unmanned supply deliveries to frontline troops. On 17 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the limit applies in Ukraine but not in European Union (EU) countries, calling it “a planned operation”. The order reportedly came from inside the White House at the suggestion of SpaceX owner Elon Musk, although US President Donald Trump has denied that either of them was responsible, and Musk has said such limits are decided by the US military. Then, on 18 October, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that Ukraine “do not have access to [Starshield] at this moment”, and that Ukrainian requests to access the system for strikes deep inside Russia are “under discussion”.
These events come amid another sharp deterioration in relations between Washington and Kyiv, after Trump agreed to a deal to import Russian diesel and demanded that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries. Starlink has been central to Ukraine’s war effort since 2022, and European governments pay for much of it: Poland alone has supplied 24,400 terminals, around half of those now operating in the country.
On 15 October, Bloomberg reported that the Commission is preparing to fast-track approval of Project Bromo, which would combine the space divisions of Airbus, Leonardo, and Thales into a single company. The venture would have around 25,000 staff and an annual revenue of about EUR 6.5b (USD 7.3b), and be headquartered in Toulouse. If the companies offer remedies such as asset sales to ease critics’ concerns, approval for the merger is likely to follow a first-phase review of just over a month, well ahead of the second half of 2027, as Leonardo had previously expected.
In the short term, Europe cannot replace Starlink in Ukraine at scale. Zelenskyy has said that European partners are working on an alternative, and that Ukraine also has plans for its own constellation, but neither will be ready in time to affect the war’s course this winter. Ukraine and European militaries are highly likely to remain dependent on US-controlled satellite services for frontline communications until at least 2030.
Implications
The restriction highlighted that Ukraine’s battlefield communications can be degraded within hours, without warning, by a decision made across the world. And while European governments fund a large share of Ukraine’s access to the technology, they have little to no say over how it is used. The operational risk is especially acute because Starlink, with around 42,000 terminals in Ukraine by early 2025, underpins much of the country’s drone warfare, from interceptor drones to supply deliveries for frontline troops.
The merger consolidates satellite manufacturing, where Airbus, Thales and Leonardo currently compete for a limited number of institutional contracts. However, it is not intended to create a single European operator of a mass low-orbit network. Starlink has more than 10,000 satellites in orbit, while IRIS², the EU’s sovereign alternative, will have 348, with first launches scheduled for 2029. Until then, Europe’s main option is Eutelsat’s OneWeb network. In 2025, France raised its stake in Eutelsat to around 30%, and its armed forces signed a contract worth up to EUR 1b (USD 1.1b) for priority military access to OneWeb. Nonetheless, the network is a fraction of Starlink’s size, with around 650 satellites currently operational.
The merger is also an early test of the Commission’s draft revised merger guidelines, published in April 2026, which give more weight to scale, supply-chain resilience, and defence considerations. Yet EU Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera has cautioned that the project “would not receive automatic approval”. Germany’s satellite manufacturer OHB and Spain’s Indra Space have objected that the merged group would dominate smaller suppliers, and OHB’s chief executive has said the company will consider legal action if Brussels approves the deal.
These tensions sit within a broader rush by the EU to spend on satellite-related capabilities. European military space investment is expected to exceed USD 109b by 2030, with Germany committing EUR 35b (USD 39b) over five years and France EUR 10.2b (USD 11.4b) for 2026-2030. However, without coordination, this spending may amount to “an aggregation of national systems, rather than an integrated operational architecture”. A single Airbus-Thales-Leonardo champion alongside separate German, French and British national programmes would fit this pattern.
Forecast
- Short-term (Now - 3 months)
  - Washington is likely to restore Ukraine’s full Starshield access only partially or conditionally, keeping satellite services as leverage in its dealings with Kyiv. 
    - European governments are likely to fund additional OneWeb terminals for Ukraine as a stopgap, despite the network’s far smaller capacity.
  - The Bromo Project partners are highly likely to file with the Commission within weeks, and the deal is likely to be cleared in a first-phase review with remedies.
- Medium-term (3 - 12 months)
  - There is a realistic possibility that OHB challenges the approval before the EU’s General Court, deepening intra-EU friction over defence industrial policy.
- Long-term (>1 year)
  - The episode is likely to strengthen both European-content requirements in EU defence procurement, especially for space services, and the broader case for European strategic autonomy in future debates over EU defence spending.

articles.title: Infineon to establish Europe's first volume 300mm GaN facility - Compound Semiconductor
articles.summary: Infineon to establish Europe's first volume 300mm GaN facility  Compound Semiconductor
articles.full_text:
Infineon is establishing the world’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next-generation GaN power semiconductors on 300mm wafers in Europe. As part of the project, Infineon will invest around €1.1 billion in its existing cleanroom facilities at the Villach site in Austria by 2034.
Production is scheduled to start by the end of 2027. Infineon’s investment addresses the rapidly growing demand for high-performance power supply solutions. GaN enables significant efficiency gains in numerous applications, such as AI data centres, energy infrastructure, e-mobility, robotics and consumer electronics.
'By establishing high-volume manufacturing on 300mm wafers, we will be the first company in the world to bring GaN power electronics into volume production,” says Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies AG. “In doing so, we are paving the way for the widespread use of GaN in a wide range of key applications in areas such as artificial intelligence, energy infrastructure, e- mobility and robotics. This new, state-of-the-art manufacturing facility translates innovation leadership into direct customer benefits.”
Christian Stocker, Federal Chancellor of the Republic of Austria: “With Infineon’s billion-euro investment, we are witnessing one of the largest single investments in the history of Austria’s high- tech industry. This is not only a strong commitment to Austria as a business location but also helps ensure that the future of the semiconductor industry will not be shaped solely in Asia or the United States, but also in Austria and Europe."
The investment is being supported under the European Chips Act. The European Commission approved €319 million in state aid. The formal funding commitment by the Austrian Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs, Energy and Tourism is expected within the stipulated time limits.

SK hynix posted operating profit of 83.3338 trillion won in the third quarter, up 632.1% from a year earlier and 37.6% from the previous quarter.
The result marks not only a record high for SK hynix (000660.KS) but an unprecedented showing among global technology giants.
The operating profit ranks third worldwide among global tech giants, trailing recently reported figures from Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) at 107.4 trillion won and Nvidia at $63.7 billion, or 84.6 trillion won. Apple had previously held third place with $50.9 billion, or 67.6 trillion won.
Its operating margin reached 79.7%, the second-highest among global tech giants after Micron's 80.7%. SK hynix's operating margin has climbed steadily on rising memory prices, from 72% in the first quarter to 76.3% in the second.

articles.title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
articles.summary: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers. articles.full_text:
Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers.



Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how.







That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business.



The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth.



Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage



Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant. Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful.



For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record. They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made. Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated.



When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor. More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows.



But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity. Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products.



When intelligence participates in action



Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world. By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor. Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action. Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions.







Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station. Vision can help the system assess a part’s position. A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement. Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits. The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately.



The same principle applies to quality operations. When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers. The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%. The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in.



This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential. Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment.



Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment. Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment. That does not remove the need for physical validation, but it creates room to learn without treating the production line as the first experiment.



Responsible deployment, therefore, begins with operational discipline. Leaders need to establish clear authority or what systems may change, reliable connections to equipment, defined safety boundaries, and a record of decisions and actions. People must be able to recognize uncertainty, intervene, and bring equipment to a safe state. Trust rests on those practical arrangements, not on confidence in a model alone.



More capable machines, more capable people



Manufacturing has long combined human ingenuity with increasingly capable tools. Physical AI extends that relationship. Intelligent equipment can take on suitable repetitive or physically demanding tasks, while agent-assisted operations can help people navigate information-intensive decisions and changing conditions.



The aim is not to make machines smarter; it is to see what people can build when knowledge can travel, intelligence can act, and ambition has more room to become reality.



Rockwell Automation illustrates the point. At its Singapore plant, technicians use a maintenance copilot that combines manufacturing data, machine manuals, and knowledge captured from experienced workers. This system has reduced the time required for new workers to learn how to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three. An engineer could explore more process alternatives before committing to a change. An operator could help improve the system’s response rather than repeatedly managing the same exception.



This type of progress requires investment in equipment but also in people: training, time to learn, and playing a meaningful role in shaping how systems work. Machines become more capable so people can become more capable.



Industrial Intelligence is the answer to sustainable growth



Industrial intelligence connects what a manufacturer knows: the experience of its people, the signals from its operations, and the lessons accumulated over time. Physical AI gives that intelligence a way to act in the physical world, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action.



The next challenge for industry is not simply to produce more, but to grow without adding complexity at the same rate. Intelligence can help manufacturers turn experience into scalable capability—improving productivity, accelerating innovation, expanding capacity, and enabling people to solve problems that were previously difficult to tackle.



The next frontier of industry is not smarter machines or more automated factories; it is businesses that can continuously learn, adapt, and act. The opportunity is to turn the intelligence embedded in every operation into a compounding advantage for growth.

articles.title: Phantom Blade Zero is asking players to free up 300GB of space for pre-loading, double its actual 145GB file size - Eurogamer.net
articles.summary: Phantom Blade Zero is asking players to free up 300GB of space for pre-loading, double its actual 145GB file size  Eurogamer.netPhantom Blade Zero Review: Wuxian Wonder Abounds  Game InformerPhantom Blade Zero’s Combat Is So Good, You Won’t Care The Story Makes No Sense  GameSpotPhantom Blade Zero PC Performance Benchmarks – Fast-Paced Wuxia That Looks Phenomenal In Path Tracing & Boosted By NVIDIA RTX Tech  WccftechThe ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Metacritic Revi...
articles.full_text:
Pre-loads are live for Phantom Blade Zero, the debut action game from Chinese developer S-Game. Alongside news of the pre-load, the studio revealed the final set of PC requirements, including how much space the game is going to take up on your drive.
Once installed, Phantom Blade Zero will occupy a chonky 145GB of your precious storage space. However, to pre-load the game, you're going to need over double that - 300GB, seemingly for the decryption and decompression process. The developer explained in a Steam blog post that "temporary files and the complete game files must coexist during the unlock process". You'll get back the extra space once the game is installed, of course.
While a game requiring extra space for these operations is not uncommon, the fact Phantom Blade Zero's install size is already so large makes needing to free up double that ludicrous. Phantom Blade Zero also requires an SSD drive, and seeing as the global gen-AI-driven memory and storage shortages have made them unattainable to many, you're not likely to buy a new drive just to accommodate a single game.
High as they may be, those storage space requirements aren't likely to deter players from buying a copy. Indeed, the game is already predicted to be among the year's biggest hits, having already sold over 500,000 copies on Steam alone, according to some estimates.
Eurogamer reviewed Phantom Blade Zero. In her review, Emma Kent was critical of the game's underwhelming boss flights and its general lack of polish, which she said mar Phantom Blade Zero's otherwise fluid and cinematic kung fu-style action.
Phantom Blade Zero arrives 29th October on PC and PS5.

articles.title: Gene therapy that led to boy’s death had limited efficacy
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03449-6Therapy pioneered by biotechnology Chinese firm HuidaGene showed promise in animals but caused a fatal reaction in a child.

Results from the first human trial of an experimental gene-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), in which a young Chinese boy died, have been published1. Although the trial provides evidence that the treatment developed by HuidaGene, based in Shanghai, China, edited some target genes, the therapeutic benefit was limited and led to a catastrophic immune reaction in one participant. Researchers say there is an urgent need to establish safe dosages for these kinds of experimental treatment.
The trial gained attention when HuidaGene announced on 5 August that one participant, a boy, had died roughly a year earlier. Researchers criticized the company for waiting so long to publicly report the death — and the event put a spotlight on China’s fast-track clinical trials. On 27 August, HuidaGene told Nature that the firm wanted to “establish the clinical facts and undertake a comprehensive investigation” before communicating with the broader public. They said a manuscript detailing the boy’s death and post-mortem findings had been submitted to a journal in January, which has now been published in Cell.
The boy who died was one of four children to receive the experimental therapy for DMD, a progressive and ultimately fatal genetic disorder that mostly affects boys, causing difficulty in walking and gradual muscle weakening. Children with DMD have mutations in the DMD gene that affect their ability to produce dystrophin, a protein that strengthens muscle fibres. The therapy used an adeno-associated virus (AAV) to deliver a base editor — a form of CRISPR gene-editing technology — to muscles to correct the mutation. The boy who died and another boy received a high dose of the therapy in AAVs; two other boys were given a low dose.
Within 24 hours of receiving the therapy, the authors say that the boy who died experienced sudden, severe abdominal pain, followed by a fever that responded only partially to treatment. The team says his condition declined rapidly, and he developed discoloured skin due to a lack of oxygen in his blood, as well as a slow, irregular heartbeat. His heart eventually stopped, and doctors could not revive him. The authors report that an autopsy revealed that he died of acute respiratory distress syndrome, which was related to the treatment.
Ian Woodcock, a paediatric neurologist and researcher at Murdoch Children’s Research Institute in Melbourne, Australia, says the boy’s fast decline suggests it was a reaction to the dose he received. In general, a large dose of AAVs are required so the gene therapy reaches muscle cells across the body. But this increases the risk of severe immune reactions, including death, that have been reported in this and other gene therapy trials for DMD2,3. “Even though the AAV doesn't cause disease in humans, this amount of foreign invasion really triggers the immune system,” he says.
Animal studies
The authors report that they performed safety testing in cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) before the trial in people. No negative side effects were observed with either a high or low dose, but the monkeys did have a weak, short-lived immune reaction following treatment. The authors acknowledge that the monkey experiments could not detect rare side effects, such as the severe immune reaction experienced by the boy who died, because they only tested the treatment in four animals.
When asked whether they should have run tests in more animals, co-author Hui Yang, co-founder of HuidaGene, said that increasing animal numbers alone could not guarantee prediction of an uncommon reaction in people, particularly because different species have different immune responses.
The boy who died was the second to receive the high dose, and only after safety data for the other high-dose recipient and the two low-dose recipients were reviewed by the trial’s safety review committee, the authors said. The exact dosage the boys received was based on their weight.
The team said that the boy who died received a higher dose than the other boy in the high-dose group because he had a higher body mass index (BMI). But that does not necessarily mean that he had more lean muscle, which is the target of the therapy. Yang says that the boy’s muscles might have been exposed to a higher dose than in the other boys, but it is still unclear whether that could have triggered the severe immune reaction. The authors suggest that dosing on the basis of body weight might not be appropriate.
Yang says the team tried to reduced the risk of severe immune responses by giving the boys immunosuppressants, testing both doses in animals and staggering each boy’s treatment following a safety review. But given the boy’s death, those measures were insufficient, he says. “We therefore need to re-examine the assumptions underlying dose selection, the role of body composition,” and the predictive value of preclinical studies, he adds. Stronger independent safety oversight and ways of reducing the effective dose also need to be developed, he adds. “The most important lesson is that severe systemic immune toxicity following AAV administration remains difficult to predict.”
Next-generation AAVs that are better at penetrating muscles could mean that lower doses can achieve the same editing effect, says Woodcock. Or the team might consider an alternative to AAVs, he adds.

articles.title: Russia has a sustained pattern of harassing US national security space satellites: DIA - Washington Examiner
articles.summary: Russia has a sustained pattern of harassing US national security space satellites: DIA  Washington Examiner
articles.full_text:
A Russian military satellite that got dangerously close to a U.S.-registered one earlier this month is the latest in a string of similar incidents, according to a new report from the Defense Intelligence Agency.
The Russian satellite, Cosmos 2612, spent more than two weeks traveling toward ICEYE-X36, a radar satellite the American arm of the Finnish company ICEYE operates, and which supplies imagery to Ukraine’s military.
Thomas DiNanno, the undersecretary of State for Arms Control and International Security, said last week: “Russia’s COSMOS 2612 military satellite has been exhibiting threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite, behaviors consistent with on-orbit weapons operations.”
A Defense Intelligence Agency report released on Monday highlighted several similar incidents that have occurred within the past decade.
In 2019, Russia launched Cosmos 2542, and it released another satellite, Cosmos 2543, which began following “a U.S. national security satellite and approached it multiple times at a distance close enough to create potentially dangerous operating conditions,” the report said. In 2020, Cosmos 2543 moved away from the U.S. satellite and fired a projectile into orbit as a part of an anti-satellite weapons test.
Russia’s Cosmos satellite series is numbered chronologically.
In 2022, Russia launched Cosmos 2558, which also came within range of a U.S. government satellite. In May 2024, Russia launched Cosmos 2576 into the same orbit as another U.S. national security satellite and maneuvered toward it.
Then, in February of last year, Russia launched Cosmos 2581, 2582, and 2583. The satellites conducted a series of maneuvers at close proximity once they were in orbit. A Space Force fact sheet said the three satellites “conducted a series of maneuvers that enabled close approaches of under 1 km. Operations of this type could be used to threaten or collect on U.S. satellites.”
In May 2025, a couple of months later, Russia launched Cosmos 2588, and it conducted maneuvers within 60 miles of a U.S. government satellite.
In May of this year, Russia executed fuel-intensive maneuvers with Cosmos 2610-2613 — including the one that tracked a U.S. satellite earlier this month — to get closer to a western commercial radar satellite used by Ukraine as well, the Space Force fact sheet said.
Russia is also seeking to develop an anti-satellite capability using a new satellite that would be designed to carry a nuclear weapon, and that would pose a threat to all satellites and the services they provide to the world.
Space is increasingly becoming a contested domain for the U.S. and Russia, with China also expanding its space capabilities.
China, for its part, has tripled its intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance satellite fleet since 2018 to more than 510; has more than tripled its space launches per year over the past decade with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 in 2025; and Beijing has also deployed more than nine times as many satellites in orbit per year during the past eight years, going from 40 in 2016 to 384 in 2025.
The DIA report notes there is “no indication that China plans to actively test or develop a nuclear [anti-satellite] weapon for use in space,” unlike Russia.
Last month, the secretary of the Air Force, Troy Meink, publicly confirmed the U.S. has “on-orbit space control” weapons, while Gen. Douglas A. Schiess, the Chief of Space Operations, said Guardians “operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the Joint Force against space-enabled attacks.”

The U.S. Department of Defense’s intelligence agency has released a new report on the development of China’s military space capabilities, with a separate section devoted to the secret reusable spacecraft Shenlong (“Divine Dragon”). The document features a rare orbital image of the spacecraft, captured by a Maxar satellite in 2024.
Shenlong is an unmanned, reusable spacecraft launched into orbit by a launch vehicle, capable of maneuvering in space and returning to Earth using a runway, like the American space shuttles or the Soviet Buran.
According to intelligence reports, the spacecraft’s first test flight in 2020 lasted two days; but during the second and third flights, the spacecraft remained in space for more than 260 days, performing complex maneuvers involving rendezvous and manipulation of inspection satellites.
In February 2026, China launched Shenlong on its fourth mission, during which the spacecraft repeatedly released and re-captured a support satellite at a distance of several thousand kilometers. The U.S. views such tests as a means of refining technologies for inspecting, servicing, and potentially intercepting or neutralizing orbital objects. The primary U.S. counterpart to the Chinese spaceplane is the X-37B military unmanned spacecraft, which has been on its eighth classified long-duration flight since August 2025.
Source: U.S. Department of Defense Intelligence Agency report.
Beijing is concerned about the growing number of SpaceX’s Starlink satellites in the context of a potential war and is seeking ways to neutralize them.
Sergey Glazyev, an academician at the Russian Academy of Sciences, and Russian oligarch Konstantin Malofeev have proposed several ways to disable the Starlink satellite system used by Ukraine. Among the options they mentioned were electronic jamming, the physical destruction of satellites, the creation of space debris, and even a nuclear explosion in space.

Quantum computing has promised to transform everything from drug discovery to cybersecurity, potentially solving problems that would take today's most powerful supercomputers thousands of years. The technology has attracted billions of dollars in investment. But turning laboratory experiments into commercially useful machines remains an enormous engineering challenge.
Unlike artificial intelligence (AI), where businesses already generate revenue from commercial applications, quantum computing is still largely in its research phase. Yet progress is accelerating, and Alphabet (GOOGL) just delivered another breakthrough.

Google's latest achievement brings practical quantum computing closer, but investors shouldn't mistake a technological milestone for an imminent commercial revolution.
Google's 40-Fold Quantum Computing Breakthrough
On Oct. 15, Google Quantum AI announced that its Willow quantum processor successfully demonstrated a technique called "magic state cultivation."
The achievement sounds like something from a Harry Potter book, but the science behind it addresses quantum computing's biggest weakness: errors. Quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily fragile. Tiny disturbances can corrupt calculations, making complex computations unreliable.
Google's technique reduced errors in specially prepared quantum states by approximately 40-fold, achieving 99.99% logical fidelity for operations called T-gates. These operations are essential for performing advanced quantum calculations.
According to Google's research team, preparing these states using older methods could consume as much as 95% of a quantum computer's capacity. The breakthrough offers a potentially more efficient alternative.
There's a catch, though. The experiment retained only about 8% of attempts, and its 40-fold improvement applies specifically to magic-state errors, not the entire quantum computer.
Google has proved the technique works. It hasn't proved that it can operate economically at commercial scale.
Why 1 Million Qubits Changes Everything
Google's Willow processor contains 105 physical qubits. Its ultimate roadmap envisions approximately 1 million. The reason for that enormous difference is that physical qubits aren't the same as logical qubits.

China's biggest tech platforms are reportedly chasing memory supply contracts as long as a decade, after US hyperscalers locked up much of the available capacity
China’s three largest internet companies are trying to lock down the memory chips that power AI servers, and they are reportedly willing to sign up for a very long time to get them.
Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance are negotiating long-term supply agreements with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix for DDR5 and LPDDR5 memory. The goal is to feed a fast-growing buildout of AI data centers. The catch is that much of what they want has already been spoken for.
What the Chinese giants are asking for
The talks center on two kinds of memory. Server-grade DDR DRAM is the workhorse memory sitting next to processors in data center machines. LPDDR is the low-power variant, built to do similar work while drawing less electricity.
What stands out is the contract length. The Chinese firms are reportedly seeking deals stretching as far as 2035. Industry norms for these long-term agreements, known as LTAs, typically run 3-5 years.
The three companies are also reportedly prepared to pay premiums to guarantee reliable supply.
Why supply is so tight
The scramble makes more sense once you see the queue. US hyperscalers, including AWS, Microsoft, Google Cloud, and Meta, have already secured substantial memory supplies for their own AI servers.
Those earlier commitments have absorbed most of the available LTA capacity. That leaves Chinese buyers competing for whatever volume remains.

The numbers are stark. An estimated 70-80% of Samsung and SK Hynix’s 2027 production is already committed to existing long-term agreements. Samsung plans to allocate at least 70% of its memory output to LTAs.
Demand from China is not small, either. The country has the world’s second-largest AI data center pipeline, estimated at over 24 GW.
According to SemiAnalysis data, ByteDance is advancing approximately 5.3 GW of AI data center capacity. Alibaba is at 3.9 GW, and Tencent is at 2.4 GW.
The GPU bill is already in
Memory is only one part of the shopping list. The three Chinese firms recently placed combined orders exceeding $35 billion for Nvidia GPUs to support their AI expansion.
Securing DRAM supply is the logical next step once the processors are on order.
What this means for memory makers and the AI race
For Samsung and SK Hynix, the negotiations put them in an enviable position. They have more customers asking for long-term volume than they can comfortably serve.
Memory has historically been a boom-and-bust business, with prices swinging hard between shortage and glut. Contracts reaching toward 2035 would give the suppliers unusual visibility into future revenue, which is rare in this corner of the chip market.
For the Chinese platforms, the stakes are about keeping pace. Their US rivals moved first and claimed the bulk of available capacity. ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent are now trying to make sure their data center plans are not stalled by a memory bottleneck.
With over 24 GW of AI data center capacity in the works, demand for memory is likely to keep pressing against supply that has largely been pre-sold.

articles.title: EU moves to curb Elon Musk’s Starlink dominance with five-pronged strategy - The New Voice of Ukraine
articles.summary: EU moves to curb Elon Musk’s Starlink dominance with five-pronged strategy  The New Voice of Ukraine
articles.full_text:
The European
Union is challenging billionaire Elon Musk’s Starlink project on at least
five fronts — from restricting access and backing competitors to developing new
regulations aimed directly at undermining the tech mogul’s growing dominance in
the space industry, Politico
reported on Oct. 26.
Musk is expanding his influence in the space industry and
seeking to turn Starlink into a “major mobile network operator,” the report
said.
European governments and companies fear becoming dependent
on Musk’s technology and are stepping up efforts to counter his growing
influence, according to Politico.
“Ukraine’s dependence on Starlink highlights the vulnerability
of European defense systems that rely on American technology. This is another
reminder that Europe must reduce its dangerous technological dependence as
quickly as possible,” Finnish member of the European Parliament Aura Salla
said.
Politico outlined five ways the EU is trying to curb the
dominance of Musk’s satellites in the skies.
1. Clearing the way for a Starlink competitor
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has
backed a deal between Airbus, Leonardo and Thales to merge their satellite and
space divisions into a single large company, code-named Bromo, that could
compete with SpaceX.
“These are exactly the kind of industrial leaders we need if
Europe wants to take a leading position in the space economy of the future,”
von der Leyen said at an international space summit in Paris last month.
Politico noted that it is highly unusual for the European
Commission president to publicly support a merger that has not yet received
approval from EU antitrust regulators.
The joint venture aims to replicate part of SpaceX’s formula
for success by bringing satellite manufacturing, ground systems and space
services under one roof. However, there is no guarantee the deal will pass EU
antitrust scrutiny.
2. Keeping Musk off the airwaves
Earlier this year, the European Commission decided to
reserve critical satellite frequency bands for European operators to ensure
security and retain control over the valuable resource.
The move immediately drew criticism from Musk’s company,
Politico reported.
“This proposal creates a significant likelihood that
Europeans will be left without direct satellite connectivity or that new
European operations will cause global interference problems, including for
emergency services such as those in Ukraine,” SpaceX warned.
Starlink will still be able to apply for access to some
satellite frequencies, but the EU wants to maintain tighter control over the
resource.
3. Building a European satellite network
The EU is developing its own satellite constellation, called
IRIS, which will eventually provide governments with secure communications and
citizens with reliable broadband internet access, Politico reported.
“The war in Ukraine has shown how much Europe’s security
depends on space. And this is where Europe needs to do more; it is an urgent
need that we ourselves feel,” European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier
told reporters.
4. Providing Ukraine with an alternative to Starlink
Ukrainian troops have faced Starlink speed restrictions in
recent weeks, complicating efforts to intercept Russian attack drones and carry
out medium-range strikes, Politico reported.
The situation has increased pressure on EU officials to
allow Kyiv to use Govsatcom, an existing secure satellite communications
project involving several EU countries.
The system was launched in early 2026 and is designed to
support critical government communications until the IRIS satellite
constellation becomes operational.
Formal talks between Brussels and Kyiv began in March 2026
but have yet to produce a breakthrough, Politico reported.
The European Govsatcom system also cannot match what
Starlink offers, although it could serve as a backup.
“I don’t understand why the European Commission and the
member states have not done everything possible to reach an agreement as
quickly as possible that would allow Ukraine to benefit from it,” French member
of the European Parliament Christophe Grudler said.
5. Creating legal obstacles for Starlink
Brussels is currently working on at least three legislative
and regulatory initiatives that could hinder, slow or complicate Starlink’s
expansion in Europe.
Michał Kobosko, the European Parliament’s lead negotiator on
revisions to the bloc’s telecommunications rules, said he wants Musk to comply
with new supply chain security requirements when seeking EU authorization to
provide Starlink services.
Meanwhile, the EU’s first-ever proposed space law, currently
under discussion, would introduce new cybersecurity, space debris management
and environmental protection requirements for Starlink and other foreign
satellite operators.
Musk’s accusations against Ukrainian forces
On Oct. 24, American billionaire Elon Musk accused Ukrainian
forces of violating Starlink’s terms of service by using the system for drone
strikes that killed people, saying the “loophole” had been closed the previous
week.
“Using Starlink — a civilian commercial service — to carry
out drone strikes for the purpose of killing people was never permitted and
should not be. Starshield is a different system controlled by the U.S.
government. It is up to them to decide how to use it. The Ukrainian military
violated Starlink’s terms of service by using the system for drone strikes that
killed people. This loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a statement
posted on his social media platform X.
Musk emphasized that Starlink remains critical to Ukraine’s
defense “because it is the only system that cannot be jammed or destroyed by an
explosion.”
Following Musk’s statement, Ukrainian presidential adviser
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov called it “very strange” that Musk was unaware of
restrictions on Starlink operations in Ukraine.
According to Beskrestnov, since the winter of 2026, all
Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine, including Russian-occupied areas, have
been subject to a movement
speed limit of 70–90 kilometers per hour. Starlink satellite communications
also do not work inside Russia.
“Therefore, we are physically unable to use commercial
Starlink to carry out long- and medium-range strikes,” Beskrestnov said.
Volunteer and former adviser to the defense minister Serhii
Sternenko, responding to Musk’s accusations, said any satellite terminal
operating while in motion had to be added to a special list and connected to
the military Starshield system.
Sternenko added that using civilian Starlink for drone
missions was technically impossible and that all drone missions requiring
satellite communications could only be carried out using Starshield.
The military war may be swinging in our favor, but the information war continues.
Just as an army needs soldiers, so does a free society need its journalists to ensure that people have access to honest, trustworthy voices to understand the world around them.

articles.summary: Starlink poses a new challenge to the telecommunications industry.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
VTV.vn - Starting as a satellite internet provider, billionaire Elon Musk's Starlink is gradually expanding its ambitions into the mobile telecommunications market.
Starlink poses a new challenge to the telecommunications industry.
Starting as a satellite internet provider, Elon Musk's Starlink is gradually expanding its ambitions into the mobile telecommunications market. With advantages in capital, technology, and a large-scale satellite network, the company holds advantages that few competitors can match. However, this also raises concerns about the concentration of power in the connectivity infrastructure sector.
In a remote village in Germany, where fiber optic cables are inaccessible, Starlink satellite internet is becoming a viable option. But behind this seemingly simple connectivity service lies a massive infrastructure operating in space.
From GPS navigation and banking transactions to disaster warnings and military operations, satellites are playing an increasingly essential role in life and the economy. And Elon Musk's SpaceX holds a unique advantage: the ability to launch satellites on a scale that many competitors struggle to match. Approximately 79% of Falcon 9 rocket flights in the first eight months of this year were dedicated to deploying Starlink satellites. Launch capability is becoming a crucial competitive advantage for SpaceX.
Heinrich Kreft, an expert in international diplomacy and security, stated: "The main issue now is who has the capability to launch satellites and who has the funding. These factors are determining how the space sector operates."
That advantage is being translated into commercial power. Starlink reached 13.6 million consumer subscribers by the end of September. The company is also expanding into direct mobile connectivity with smartphones. However, Starlink's growing scale also raises the question: What happens when a crucial part of the information infrastructure relies too heavily on the decisions of a single company?
Heinrich Kreft, an expert in international diplomacy and security, added: "Satellite connectivity is like electricity and water. The most important thing is reliability, meaning we must be able to use the service whenever we need it."
The conflict in Ukraine has shown how reliance on satellite connectivity can directly impact military operations. Disruptions to Starlink services have hampered communication and the operation of drones. Meanwhile, competitors like Amazon Leo are also building their own satellite networks. However, the gap in deployment scale and launch capacity remains a significant challenge. From a solution to bring internet to remote areas, Starlink is becoming a formidable force in the telecommunications industry.
You may also like
The telecommunications alliance enhances competitiveness.
Faced with Starlink's ambitions to expand its satellite mobile services, major telecommunications companies in Europe have begun exploring collaboration options to enhance their competitiveness.
Four telecommunications giants – Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica, and Vodafone – have agreed to study the possibility of jointly bidding for satellite spectrum rights in Europe. The goal is to develop direct satellite-mobile phone connectivity, reducing reliance on providers outside the region. Instead of building their own satellite network, the companies plan to collaborate with a satellite technology provider. The plan is currently in the preparatory stage. This move comes as the European Union increasingly emphasizes autonomy over digital infrastructure, data security, and the ability to maintain essential information services.
The European telecommunications industry assesses Starlink's prospects.
The arrival of Starlink in the mobile market is forcing traditional carriers to reconsider their strategies. However, can a satellite network truly replace millions of terrestrial base stations? In Europe, the answer remains debated.
With near-total coverage, millions of customers, and infrastructure built over decades, traditional mobile operators in Europe have a significant advantage. Therefore, even though Starlink is entering the mobile market, not all businesses believe their position will be challenged anytime soon.
Frederic Ufer, CEO of VATM telecommunications company, shared: "We need to take this seriously and have reason to be concerned. But whether Starlink will truly become a major threat as some predict remains to be seen, because existing businesses already have a very strong foothold."
One reason is coverage. In Germany and many European countries, terrestrial mobile networks already reach most of the territory. Building an additional parallel network is not easily economically advantageous. But in mountainous areas, islands, or sparsely populated regions, the problem is completely different. The cost of building and maintaining base stations can be very high compared to the number of customers served.
You may also like
Bernd Sorries, a mobile communications expert, commented: "If we want to eliminate areas without coverage, we need to use the most efficient and cost-effective technology. Satellites are certainly well-suited for covering both small and larger areas."
Therefore, network operators are not only seeking to compete but also proactively collaborating with satellite companies. Deutsche Telekom has signed an agreement with Starlink to supplement connectivity in areas with limited coverage in Europe, with deployment expected from 2028. This means that instead of replacing terrestrial networks, satellites will be used as an additional layer of connectivity. However, the story doesn't end with business efficiency. As communications increasingly become essential infrastructure, Europe must also consider the risk of dependence on foreign technology and companies.
Frederic Ufer, CEO of VATM telecommunications company, stated : "We need a solution that guarantees Europe's digital sovereignty, to maintain standards of data protection, privacy, and personal rights. This can only be achieved through European providers."
The competition, therefore, is not simply a race to see who has wider coverage. Network operators must find ways to maintain control over customers, infrastructure, and data, while still leveraging new technologies. And although it cannot yet replace traditional mobile networks, Starlink has prompted long-established businesses to prepare for a future where connectivity is no longer entirely dependent on terrestrial base stations.
Regardless of how the competition between Starlink and traditional carriers unfolds, consumers could be among the beneficiaries. Satellite connectivity promises to narrow signal gaps, especially in mountainous and island regions, or when natural disasters disrupt terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure. However, this technology currently has limitations in terms of capacity, speed, and usage conditions. More importantly, the emergence of a new provider doesn't necessarily mean an immediate price reduction. Ultimately, what users need is a stable, affordable, and reliable connection at all times.

IBM Introduces Identity and Control for AI Agents, Securing Frontier Intelligence for the Enterprise
ATLANTA, GA, Oct. 27, 2026 -- At TechXchange 2026, IBM (NYSE: IBM) is announcing new capabilities to help developers, IT and security teams put AI agents to work across business systems with clear authority and accountability. IBM brings together agent discovery, verified identities, access controls and performance evaluation to help organizations understand who owns each agent, control what it can access, and trace its actions across existing applications and infrastructure.
According to Gartner, by 2028 the average Fortune 500 enterprise will use over 150,000 AI agents. But only 13% of organizations believe that they have the right AI agent governance in place [1]. Persistent credentials, unclear ownership and disconnected controls make it harder to govern agents as they interact with other agents, invoke tools and act across teams, platforms and clouds.
“The winners in enterprise AI are changing how their business runs, not simply adding more AI to it,” said Dinesh Nirmal, Senior Vice President, IBM Software. “For agents to take on real work across the systems a company depends on, it requires an AI operating model – one that connects agents to the business’s data, applications and infrastructure and runs them with the same discipline as its most critical systems. Build trust and control into that model, and agents stop being a technology and become a way of doing business.”  
Today’s announcements extend IBM’s portfolio to deliver an AI operating model of four essential systems working together: agents, data, automation and hybrid infrastructure. This starts with the trust and control every agent needs – a verified identity, only the access it needs, and one place to discover, secure and evaluate agents regardless of where they were built.
Extending HashiCorp Vault to AI agents
HashiCorp Vault manages the secrets and credentials that applications and services use to access business systems. It provides that control through centrally managed secrets, automated rotation for supported credentials, and dynamically generated credentials that expire or can be revoked. These capabilities help reduce the time exposed credentials remain usable and limit access to the permissions configured for each role.
HashiCorp Vault already secures non-human identities for organizations including ABN AMRO, Adobe, athenahealth, BBVA, BlackRock, Canva, Duke Energy, Expedia, London Stock Exchange, Starbucks, Swiss Federal Railways and Target, across systems that process billions of dollars in transactions [2]. HashiCorp will now extend those capabilities to AI agents, issuing secured, short-lived credentials that limit each agent to what it needs.
Establishing agent identity and accountability
AI agents are a growing class of non-human identity, alongside applications and services. As they begin acting across business systems, enterprises need a clear record of who owns each agent and what authority it has been granted. HashiCorp is combining governed agent identity with credential controls to help organizations delegate work with defined authority and accountability.
When used with HashiCorp Vault, Agent Identity establishes the authoritative record for each agent, such as who owns it, its lifecycle status and the authority it has been granted. Built to extend existing identity and security investments, it shares relevant identity and authorization context with Vault’s credential controls – ultimately enforcing least-privilege access and enabling real-time revocation when an agent attempts an unauthorized action.
Controlling agent credentials and access
Identifying an agent is only the start. Enterprises also need to control the credentials it uses to reach databases, applications and cloud services – and how long those credentials remain valid.
As agents invoke tools and act across business systems, their credentials become a critical security boundary. An agent with a long-lived, overprivileged credential can put systems and data at risk if it’s compromised or acts outside its intended task. Enterprises need to establish what each agent’s job is, limit the access it receives and revoke that access when circumstances change.
These controls extend beyond initial authentication. If an agent attempts to retrieve information or perform actions outside its approved permissions, the access can be denied and session revoked in real time to prevent unauthorized activity. Vault's short-lived credentials and least-privilege controls can further restrict what an agent accesses and the duration of those permissions.
Additional capabilities include:
- Vault 2.2 gives agents their own secured accounts, automatically renews their credentials and incorporates post-quantum encryption for quantum-era threats.
- Secure Hub (public preview) gives companies centralized visibility across their Vault environments to make it easier to understand operational health, usage and security resources.
At TechXchange, client speakers will share how they use Vault to secure enterprise applications, workloads and AI agents

- Albert Einstein College of Medicine: Applying IBM Verify and Vault to AI agent identity, just-in-time access, dynamic secrets and auditability.
- Optum: Using Vault Radar to detect exposed secrets and Boundary for just-in-time, identity-based access.
- Seven-Eleven Japan: Centralizing and encrypting secrets with Vault Enterprise and detecting hardcoded secrets with Vault Radar.
- Yum! Brands: Building an identity security platform with IBM Verify, with a look ahead to machine identities and secrets management.
“AI presents extraordinary opportunities to accelerate biomedical research and discovery, but realizing its potential requires a foundation of security, trust, and responsible governance,” said Shailesh M. Shenoy, Assistant Dean for Information Technology at Albert Einstein College of Medicine. “In my experience, technologies such as IBM Verify and HashiCorp Vault can play an important role in helping organizations establish the identity, access, and security controls needed to innovate with confidence.”  
Managing agents across platforms
Identity tells organizations what an agent is. But they also need to see every agent they have, wherever it was built. IBM watsonx Orchestrate works across the AI ecosystem, not inside a single vendor’s platform, to give organizations one place to discover, secure and evaluate their agents. Capabilities include:
- Discover (tech preview): Organizations can’t govern agents they don’t know exist. Orchestrate connects to platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry and Google Gemini to find agents built in third-party environments, so teams can see and manage agents instead of adding them manually. This capability also extends to models and MCP servers.
- Contain (tech preview): One rogue agent can disrupt others and spread mistakes across the business. Orchestrate now runs agents in isolated sandboxes so a rogue agent can’t interfere with others. Teams also now have access to a kill switch to shut down any agent.
- Evaluate: Agents that aren’t tested and tracked can quietly drift off course and increase costs. Teams using Orchestrate can now test the quality, accuracy and compliance of agents, models and MCP servers before deployment, then monitor them in production. Built-in cost tracking shows each agent’s model and token use, so teams can spot what’s driving spend and fix it.
Orchestrate also works with Vault’s credential controls and Agent Identity to establish what each agent’s job is, govern its authority and enforce least-privilege credential access. Together, these controls help organizations authorize and audit agent actions and rapidly revoke trust and credentials when risk changes.
Connecting agents to the business
Once agents are authorized to use a company’s APIs and tools, they need to know what already exists, how systems connect, what can be reused safely and what their actions could affect. IBM Integration Intelligence Hub is built to provide that knowledge through its Unified Context Engine, so agents can fix problems like stuck messages or deploy an API using what’s already in place. Skills, approval policies and audit controls keep those actions in check. Instead of rebuilding for AI, organizations can put agents to work on the systems they already depend on.
Scaling agents with NVIDIA
Agent Identity and HashiCorp Vault integrate with NVIDIA OpenShell secure runtime software, the foundation of the NVIDIA OpenShell Architecture. Together, they pair a protected environment for agents to run in with a verified identity and short-lived credentials for every agent, so each action can be traced, limited and reviewed.
“Businesses need enforceable control over how agents operate and what they can access,” said John Fanelli, vice president, enterprise software, NVIDIA. “Our work with IBM combines NVIDIA OpenShell’s policy-governed runtime with Agent Identity and HashiCorp Vault to help enterprises scale AI agents with secure execution, verified identities and tightly scoped access to business systems.”

articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Will the real Anthropic please stand up?



After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and how it believes it will change the world.



But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture, presenting it as different things to different people: an AI safety organization, a profit-driven megacorp, and a group hell-bent on creating superhuman technology.



These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? Take a new glimpse inside Anthropic.



—Will Douglas Heaven



This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.



How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom



Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping efficiently move power across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.



As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses.



The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.



Find out how solid-state transformers could help meet rising electricity demand.



—Casey Crownhart



Are we there yet? Exercise in a pill



We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks, without the workout.



The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.



Discover how close researchers are to developing an exercise pill.



—Cassandra Willyard



This story is part of “Are we there yet?”  from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review. The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 Anthropic has filed for its blockbuster IPOThe listing could determine the future of the AI investment boom. (CNBC)+ The filing warns of catastrophic AI risks and huge compute costs. (BBC)+ And exposes safety failures and a month-long training pause. (Reuters $)+ The prospectus reveals soaring revenues but also staggering losses. (NYT $)+ Anthropic’s founders will retain voting control after the IPO. (Verge) 



2 Solar is quietly overtaking nuclear as a global power sourceCheap panels and batteries are accelerating the shift. (BBC)+ The balcony solar boom is coming to the US. (MIT Technology Review)



3 OpenAI has announced three new science discoveriesThey span mathematics, computer science, and physics. (Verge)+ It’s enlisted expert “shepherds” to publish its breakthroughs. (Gizmodo)



4 Microsoft is offering buyouts to a quarter of staff amid rising AI costsAround 60,000 employees are eligible for the buyout program. (Bloomberg $)+ Microsoft plans $190 billion in AI spending this year. (NYT $)



5 The plastics industry knew microplastics could enter the body decades agoCompany documents reveal concerns dating back to 1974. (LA Times $)+ No part of the globe is free of human fingerprints. (MIT Technology Review) 



6 A demonstration of lighting Earth from space has sparked alarmStartup Reflect Orbital used space mirrors for the California test. (Guardian)+ The tech could jeopardize the night sky. (MIT Technology Review)



7 The US has designated helium a critical materialThe move is due to its importance to semiconductor production. (AP)



8 Hundreds of Boston Dynamics staff have protested its ICE dealThey’ve called for a halt to sales of the robot dogs. (Ars Technica)



9 Treatments for age-related infertility are being developed at lastTwo startups aim to reduce chromosome errors in eggs. (Economist $)+ Here’s how tech transformed babymaking. (MIT Technology Review)



10 Grok says its AI-generated Odyssey is “not historically accurate”The bot itself admitted Elon Musk’s filmmaking plan has failed. (Wired $)



Quote of the day



“It’s as if they’re making a promise and crossing their fingers behind their backs.”



 —Kate Brennan, who leads policy at the AI Now Institute, tells the New York Times that the voluntary safety pledges AI executives recently made are toothless and unenforceable.



One more thing



MCKIBILLO




The problem with thinking you’re part Neanderthal



There’s a theory that many of us have an “inner Neanderthal.” The idea is that Homo sapiens and its cousin species once bred, leaving some people today with a trace of Neanderthal DNA. 



This DNA is arguably the 21st century’s most celebrated discovery in human evolution. But in 2024, a pair of French geneticists called into question the theory’s very foundations. 



They proposed that what scientists interpret as interbreeding could instead be explained by population structure—the way genes concentrate in smaller, isolated groups.



Find out what it all means for human evolution.



—Ben Crair

articles.title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
articles.summary: International travel used to be the main risk of measles cases in the US—not anymore.
articles.full_text:
Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country's occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely — or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions.
In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread.
South Carolina's measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania's ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it.Read full article

articles.title: [不同来源] Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
articles.summary: Critical flaw in EDK2 allows attackers to execute code early in the boot process.
articles.full_text:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.
The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the "preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications." Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft's hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.Read full article

articles.title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software
articles.summary: You can apparently now tell AI tools what sort of protein you want them to make.
articles.full_text:
Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated, but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target.
A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it's now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level.
The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones.Read full article

articles.full_text:
This morning, Ford revealed that buyers of the forthcoming Fathom—the company's sub-$30,000 electric pickup truck due next year—will get more than just a truck. Until now, vehicle-to-home technology—like the setup Ford developed for the now-discontinued F-150 Lightning—takes DC power from the electric vehicle and runs it through an inverter built into the wallbox to turn it into AC the house can use. But with the Fathom, that inverter is built into the truck from the start. So every Fathom will be able to act as a backup battery for your home.
It’s typical: You wait a decade for a cheap electric truck, and then two come along almost at once. And they’re two radically different products from two radically different automakers that I think will reveal a few preferences from the EV-buying public. One is the Blank Slate, from a brand new startup offering a bare-bones two-door that capitalizes on features the Internet says it wants, like no onboard modem, no touchscreens, and no infotainment system.
The other is the result of one of Detroit’s big three taking a long, hard look at Chinese EVs and asking itself, “How do we make a car that cheap?” Although the Ford Fathom will cost $5,000 more than a Slate, that money does buy an extra pair of doors, modern conveniences like an infotainment system, CarPlay, electric windows, and a vast dealership network to service the car. That may be helpful given how many recalls Ford issues each year.Read full article

articles.title: Sculpture re-creates odd optical effects of famed Lycurgus Cup
articles.summary: University of Sheffield researchers figured out how to re-create the 1,600-year-old glass recipe.
articles.full_text:
Dating back to around 400 CE and made of dichroic glass, the Lycurgus Cup is notable for exhibiting different colors depending on the light. (It gets its name from the scene depicted on its surface, of King Lycurgus of Thrace.) Light it from the front, and the cup looks green; light it from behind, and the color changes to a deep red. University of Sheffield scientists have re-created the original recipe to produce a contemporary glass sculpture with the same optical effect.
The cup is considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world, one of just 40 glass cage cups that survived. Exactly why the unusual color effects of the Lycurgus Cup occurred was a mystery until 2007, when a team of scientists discovered the color shifts were due to the presence of nanoparticles in the glass—the result of Roman artisans adding finely ground gold and silver into the mix. Those nanoparticles change how the electrons in the cup vibrate in response to light so that the color one sees shifts with the observer’s vantage point.
As we reported in 2019, it’s a similar phenomenon to the one responsible for the shifting colors of 19th-century daguerreotypes due to the scattering properties of nanoparticles. The Romans added salt when they melted the silicon (sand) to make the glass, and those salts contained gold atoms. In the melting process, those atoms aggregate and produce nanoparticles, which in turn produce the colors. It’s how any stained glass is made. It's also similar to how the precise lattice-like structure of photonic crystals produces iridescent colors in nature, like the wings of butterflies, or opals.Read full article
